news.title: Map Shows Democrat, Republican Voter Registration Shifts 38 Days to Midterm
news.text: Democrats have cut into Republicans' voter registration advantage in several states with competitive Senate races ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, though Republicans retain advantages in some of the conservative states that appear increasingly competitive. The race for Senate control appears increasingly competitive ahead of the November 3 elections, with Democrats leading some polls in more conservative states like Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas, all of which backed President Donald Trump by double digits in 2024. Democrats are increasingly hopeful that they can expand the electoral battleground to compete in these states that have historically been more difficult. This is largely due to Trump’s approval rating falling to new lows in polling this week amid frustrations with the economy, cost of living and soaring gas prices amid the Iran war. Voter registration data can reveal changes in states’ partisan composition, but it’s not always predictive of how a state will vote, particularly during a wave year when one party is benefiting from a strong national environment. These numbers can be influenced by factors including population shifts, migration patterns, the removal of inactive voters from voter rolls and people leaving a party when they are dissatisfied with its direction. Notably, not all states have registration by party. Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota, Ohio and Texas all have fairly competitive races this year, but there is no partisan registration in those states. Stephen Farnsworth, political science professor at the University of Mary Washington, told Newsweek that voters “often punish the president’s party in midterm elections.” Trump’s unusually low approval rating is making things worse for Republicans compared to the usual midterm pain for the party in the White House, he said. “Angry voters are more engaged as shown in the latest registration figures. A lot of young people in particular worry about the availability of good jobs in the face of growing AI, which is another policy area where Trump is out of step with voters,” Farnsworth said. Where Democrats Are Gaining There are several states where Democrats have narrowed the gap in voter registration that also have competitive Senate races this year, though Republicans do hold advantages in each of these states. Alaska The gap has slightly narrowed in Alaska, where GOP Senator Dan Sullivan is facing a challenge from former Representative Mary Peltola. In December 2025, Republicans had a 73,829 advantage on the voter rolls. That had narrowed to a 72,290-voter advantage in September 2026, according to the Alaska Division of Elections. Polls show a tight race in the state, which backed Trump by about 13 points in the 2024 election. Alaska has been viewed as a reliably Republican stronghold, but a leftward shift in cities like Anchorage has loosened the GOP’s grip on the state. The latest Alaska Survey Research poll showed a tight race, with Peltola leading Sullivan in the final round of ranked-choice, 50.6 percent to 49.4 percent. It surveyed 1,495 likely voters from August 20 to 23 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Peltola had a larger lead in a poll from Data for Progress, which surveyed 578 likely voters July 28-August 4. It showed Peltola up 6 points, 53 percent to 47 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. However, a poll from The New York Times and Siena University, conducted among 593 likely voters June 15-29, showed Sullivan up 2 points, 47 percent to 45 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. The Cook Political Report classifies the race as a toss up. Newsweek reached out to the Peltola and Sullivan campaigns for comment via email. Iowa In Iowa, a former battleground that has become more conservative over the past decade, Democrats have also been able to chip away at Republicans’ advantage. In December 2025, there were 196,755 more Republicans than Democrats in Iowa. As of September 2026, that number was 182,715. Iowa also backed Trump by about 13 points in 2024, as Republicans have made gains among the state’s rural, white population. Democrats have failed to make up those losses in suburban areas around cities like Des Moines. But the Senate race between Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state Representative Josh Turek appears competitive. A new poll from Marist University gave Turek an 8-point advantage, 50 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 1,050 registered voters from September 17 to 20, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points. However, Hinson led the latest survey from co/efficient by 4 points, 46 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 831 likely voters from September 14 to 16, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.39 percentage points. Turek also led Hinson in a recent YouGov poll. He had a single-point lead, 44 percent to 43 percent, among registered voters, but led by 4 points, 47 percent to 43 percent, among "strict” likely voters. The poll surveyed 2,169 registered voters from September 3 to 8. Its margin of error was plus or minus 3.5 percent among registered and likely voters. The Cook Political Report classifies the race as a toss up. Newsweek reached out to the Hinson and Turek campaigns for comment via email. Kansas The Kansas Senate race appears increasingly competitive, with the Cook Political Report this week shifting it from Likely Republican to Leans Republican. Republicans have a sizable advantage of 394,642 voters in Kansas, down from 401,710 in November 2025, according to the Kansas secretary of state office. The Sunflower State backed Trump by 16 points in 2024. But it does have a Democratic governor, and suburban areas around Kansas City have narrowed Republican margins in statewide contests. Republican Senator Roger Marshall is up for reelection and is facing Democrat Adam Hamilton, a pastor. A recent poll from Emerson College was a statistical tie, with Hamilton receiving 45 percent and Marshall 43 percent. It surveyed 750 likely voters from September 15 to 16, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. A co/efficient poll also pointed to a close race, giving Marshall a 5-point lead, 49 percent to 44 percent. It surveyed 915 likely voters from September 8 to 10, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.22 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to the Hamilton and Marshall campaigns for comment via email. Nebraska Republican Senator Pete Ricketts is facing a challenge from independent candidate Dan Osborn in Nebraska. Osborn has said he would not caucus with either party in Washington, but he will need strong support from Democrats and independents, as well as some moderate Republicans, to win in November. There are 292,049 more registered Republicans than Democrats in Nebraska, down from 294,750 in 2025, according to the Nebraska secretary of state office. Nebraska voted for Trump by more than 20 points in 2024. Forecasters give Ricketts an advantage, with the Cook Political Report rating the race as Likely Republican. Polls show a close race. A SurveyUSA poll showed Osborn up 4 points, 46 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 503 likely voters from September 8 to 13, with a credibility interval of plus or minus 6.4 percentage points. An Impact Research poll, an Osborn internal, showed an even race, each receiving 47 percent of the vote. It surveyed 600 likely voters from August 9 to 13, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. It was first reported by The Omaha World Herald. Newsweek reached out to the Osborn and Ricketts campaigns for comment via email. New Hampshire Republicans also have an advantage in New Hampshire, though it backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 3 points in 2024. Independent voters are key to the Granite State, viewed as having a moderate electorate with a libertarian streak. Republicans have a 43,022-voter registration advantage in the state, down from a 49,635 advantage in 2025, according to the New Hampshire secretary of state office. The Senate race between Representative Chris Pappas and former Senator John Sununu is viewed as a toss-up by the Cook Political Report as polls suggest a closely divided electorate. The latest survey from InsiderAdvantage showed Pappas up 8 points, 48 percent to 40 percent. It polled 1,200 likely voters from September 16 to 17, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. A survey from GOP pollster Fabrizio, Lee & Associates showed the race in a statistical tie, with Sununu receiving 37 percent support and Pappas 36 percent. Other candidates received less than 4 percent support, while 23 percent were undecided about who they would vote for. Another poll from the University of New Hampshire poll similarly showed Sununu with a lead, 45 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 1,878 likely voters August 20-24 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.3 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to the Pappas and Sununu campaigns for comment via email. Where Republicans Are Gaining There are two competitive states where Republicans have gained ground in voter registration. Maine In Maine, where Senator Susan Collins is facing a competitive race against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former president of the Maine Senate, Republicans have gained a bit of ground, but Democrats still have an advantage on the voter rolls. Democrats had a 31,732 advantage in the state as of March, a shift from 43,755 in 2025, according to the secretary of state office. The Senate race is expected to be one of the most competitive of the midterms, with the Cook Political Report viewing it as a toss up. Recent polls pointed to a close race. A survey from The New York Times and Siena College showed Collins with a 3-point lead, 49 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 619 likely voters from September 15 to 22, 2026. Another poll from the University of Massachusetts Lowell published on Thursday gave Jackson a 5-point lead, 48 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 650 likely voters from August 28 to September 14, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.66 percentage points. A Quantus Insights poll showed a statistical tie, with Collins at 47.1 percent and Jackson at 46.4 percent. It surveyed 644 likely voters from September 14 to September 15, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.3 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to the Collins and Jackson campaigns for comment via email. North Carolina Democrats have also lost ground in North Carolina, where former Governor Roy Cooper, a Democrat, is viewed as a favorite over Republican Michael Whatley. The Cook Political Report classifies the race as Leans Democratic. In 2025, Democrats had a mere 604 vote advantage. That has flipped to Republicans, who had a 7,403-vote advantage in the state as of September, according to the North Carolina State Board of Elections. Jeff Allen, a spokesperson for Cooper’s campaign, told Newsweek that North Carolina “is a 50-50 state,” casting the election as a “margin-of-error race.” “A Democrat has not won statewide federal office here in nearly two decades – and Whatley’s elite DC connections mean Republicans are going to spend whatever it takes to keep this seat,” Allen said. Newsweek also reached out to the Whatley campaign for comment via email. Polls have given Cooper a lead. A Quantus Insights poll showed him up 5 points, 48 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 686 likely voters from September 21 to 22, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.2 percentage points. Cooper led by 11 points in a YouGov poll, which surveyed 3,895 registered voters from September 15 to 18 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points. Cooper’s support stood at 52 percent, while 41 percent of respondents said they would vote for Whatley among registered voters. Democrats’ Chances of Flipping the Senate Farnsworth said that Democrats’ prospects “for taking over the Senate are better than 50-50.” “Voters struggling with high prices want to see a president focused on that issue and trying to do something about it,” he said. “Instead they see a president who promised a more domestic focus is stuck in an unappealing stalemate with Iran, with limiting press access to public events, and on building a new White House ballroom and a massive arch near Arlington Cemetery.” Prediction markets have recently shifted momentum toward Democrats for control of the Senate in November. As of Friday, Democrats had a 61 percent chance on Kalshi and a 63 percent chance on Polymarket of flipping the Senate. That marks a shift from one month ago, when Republicans had a 53 percent chance on Kalshi, while their chances were tied on Polymarket. Republicans had even stronger chances at the start of the year, holding a 68 percent chance on Kalshi and a 66 percent chance on Polymarket of holding onto the Senate. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. What Happens Next Polls will be closely watched over the coming weeks as the race for Senate control remains close. Candidates are making their pitches to voters across their states on issues ranging from the economy and foreign policy. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Jenni Fink and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: Democrats cut into Republicans' voter registration advantage in several states with competitive Senate races.

news.title: ‘Prophet of Doom’ makes unexpected prediction about what Trump will do after presidency
news.text:
A man nicknamed as the 'Prophet of Doom' has made a prediction about what will happen to Donald Trump after he finishes his term as president.

Craig Hamilton-Parker is a psychic who has become well-known for his predictions about world events.

Over the years these have included things like the death of Queen Elizabeth II, who died in 2022 at the age of 96, as well as the coronavirus pandemic.

But now Hamilton-Parker has turned his attention to the US, speaking to VT.co about what the future may hold for Donald Trump.

One prediction in particular looks at Trump's future post-presidency, so what does Hamilton-Parker say about this?

“The key thing that I said that I thought was the strangest of all is that when he finishes his career as a politician, he will become a religious figure, religious-type figure,” Hamilton-Parker told VT.co.

He added: “And then we get this business with him dressed up like Jesus. And now we hear him speaking a bit like that as well sometimes. There's more and more of a sort of a ‘I'm here to save humanity’ sort of vibe to him."

Explaining how he gets his alleged visions, Hamilton-Parker said: "When it comes to you, you just get a feeling about it. I don't know, it comes out of the blue. It's like something just given to you.”

Hamilton-Parker even made the outlandish claim that Trump had been a Hindu priest devoted to Shiva in a past life who fell out of favour because of alcohol.

He said: “Which makes me think, was that past life? And did that past life bring kind of religious energy within him of some sort from India?”

However, other predictions that he shared with the outlet indicate that this may come later than many people might expect, saying that he predicts Trump might even serve a third term as US president, even though the US constitution limits people to two presidential terms.

Many of Trump's supporters continue to attest that he won the 2020 election against Joe Biden, claiming that the election was rigged, even though Biden won fair and square. 

If this were true though it would also mean that Trump was excluded from running again in 2024, where he beat Kamala Harris and returned to the White House.

Nonetheless, Hamilton-Parker said: “At the time of the next election in 2028, I feel - I've been saying this for a long time - that I feel that he will have a third presidency.

“There is so much going on in the world crisis-wise, and particularly with a war that will be, by that time, happening with China. So it's like, I have to take emergency measures, therefore I stay in control.”

Other predictions that Hamilton-Parker made involved dangers linked to artificial intelligence, more specifically that it would be connected to some sort of crisis in the financial sector.

It's certainly a rabbit hole to go down, but of course the only way to find out for sure what will happen is to wait and see - que será será.
news.summary: Craig Hamilton-Parker is a psychic who makes big predictions about the future
news.author: Kit Roberts

news.title: Kamala Harris is belatedly courting progressives. Is it too little, too late? | Arwa Mahdawi
news.text:
Does Donald Trump secretly want Republicans to get annihilated in the midterms? Because he’s certainly acting that way. He continues to brush off concerns about the cost of living, saying last week that high gas prices are a very “inexpensive price to pay” for the war on Iran.

And, of course, the president seems to have no plans to end that disastrous war, apart from making vague threats about blowing the entire country up. Trust me, he keeps saying, everything will get better after the midterms. But by the looks of his dismal polling numbers, not many people are swallowing his empty promises anymore.

Still, despite the mess the Republicans have made of the country, I wouldn’t feel too optimistic about the Democrats returning to power: the party is famous for snatching defeat from the jaws of victory. Instead of evolving, it has a tendency to do the same thing over and over again, expecting different results.

See, for example, the fact that there are once again loud murmurings that Kamala Harris plans to run for president in 2028. The former vice-president hasn’t made any sort of official announcement yet – she told voters in Detroit this week that she’s still deciding what to do – but she seems to be testing the political waters through midterm campaigning.

This week she flew to Michigan, one of the states she lost to Trump in 2024, to join the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a roundtable focused on Black maternal health. Harris will also be campaigning with the senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia next month and attending an event in Las Vegas with the Nevada attorney general, Aaron Ford, for his gubernatorial bid.

Harris’s appearance in Michigan wasn’t some spur-of-the-moment attempt to be helpful; it was a highly calculated move designed to put her back on the national political stage.

The New York Times reported this week that Harris’s aides had circulated a donor prospectus in July “that showed how she would try to maintain her influence atop the Democratic Party as she considered another run for president in 2028”. The document, which solicited funds for campaign travel, explained how Harris could boost midterm candidates. It also asserted that the current moment is “uniquely suited to Vice President Harris and a broad coalition already in motion”.

But not everyone agrees it’s Harris’s time to shine. Numerous Democratic candidates have publicly stated that they don’t want Harris’s toxic brand anywhere near their elections.

El-Sayed, meanwhile, seems to have decided that an alliance with Harris is mutually beneficial. It gives the progressive candidate an inroad into the establishment and might help him win more support with Black voters.

Harris, who alienated many progressives and Arab Americans by her stance on Gaza, clearly thinks that associating with El-Sayed might improve her reputation among that cohort of voters. El-Sayed has said he opposes military aid to Israel and termed the situation in Gaza a genocide – as have numerous human rights groups and genocide experts.

El-Sayed isn’t the only progressive that Harris appears to be trying to build bridges with. Last year, Harris offered only the most lukewarm of endorsements for Zohran Mamdani, stating: “He’s the Democratic nominee, and he should be supported.” Now that it’s clear that Mamdani embodies the political zeitgeist, she’s a lot more keen to be besties. In early July, Axios reported that Harris called up the New York mayor a couple of days after three leftwing candidates he’d endorsed won their primaries over establishment-backed candidates.

In fact, Harris has been working the phones pretty hard. The same Axios piece noted that she’d reached out to a number of pro-Palestinian activists and Arab American leaders including James Zogby, founder and president of the Arab American Institute. He told Slate this week that the two had had a “long talk”, which he felt good about.

In 2024, the Democrats took progressives for granted. They assumed that young progressives would show up to vote blue no matter who, even when the party treated them with disdain. Instead many of these voters stayed home.

The Democrats are still loath to admit that Gaza was a factor in their defeat: a 2024 autopsy report released by the Democratic National Committee did not mention the issue once. However, it looks like Harris is waking up to the realization that her almost unconditional support for Israel hurt her in the previous election and is something she will have to rectify if she wants to run again. Particularly since polls show a record 60% of US adults now have an unfavourable view of Israel and the vast majority of Democrats support an arms embargo.

Is all this too little too late for the former nominee’s brand? I don’t know. But it’s certainly too late for the tens of thousands of Palestinians the Biden-Harris administration were complicit in killing.

The murder of nine women causes a reckoning in South Africa

The bodies of nine women have been found across the Ekurhuleni district, east of Johannesburg, over the past two months. Some were naked or partially clothed. The apparent murders, which may be connected, have reignited protests about the country’s femicide rate, which is five times higher than the global average. Hundreds of demonstrators marched through Cape Town on Thursday, demanding an end to gender-based violence.

Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to train wins Asian Games silver

Fariba Hashimi was attacked with stones and had to train while disguised as a man when she first started cycling. Now based in Italy, Hashimi won an Asian Games silver medal on Tuesday and hopes to compete in the 2028 Los Angeles games.

A Republican senator has warned that furries are infiltrating the aviation community

“It’s terrifying when you think about this,” the senator Tommy Tuberville said this week. “When you walk onto a commercial flight, it’s possible that the pilot flying your plane could have a deranged fetish of dressing up like an animal.” Tuberville seems to be referencing an incident in April when pilots were heard making “meow” sounds over an air traffic control frequency at Ronald Reagan Washington national airport. Is it possible they were maybe just mucking around? Or have the friendly really skies been taken over by a dastardly coalition of furries?

Masked lesbian infighting went ultra-viral this week

I wrote about the Last Ditch drama here.

The dangers of AI are already here

“The future is already here – it’s just unevenly distributed,” the science fiction writer William Gibson once said. And that is very true of AI. “We don’t have to wait to see how AI will bring about unprecedented death and destruction, because we’ve already witnessed its unleashing,” Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein write in the Guardian.

Six-year-old Chinese girl ‘sets new women’s Rubik’s Cube world record’

Lian Yunzhi is reportedly “the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds”.

A day in the life of a pregnant woman in Gaza

Sitting in her tent, warding off rats, Alaa watches videos of her three children, killed in an Israeli airstrike, on her cracked smartphone. She gave birth to a new baby boy, Waseem, shortly after the Guardian published this piece.

Ed Sheeran’s shows at Gillette Stadium canceled due to nor’easter

A hilarious development in the Ed “I’m not complicit in genocide” Sheeran tour story. Even the weather is sick of hearing him whine.

 Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

And, of course, the president seems to have no plans to end that disastrous war, apart from making vague threats about blowing the entire country up. Trust me, he keeps saying, everything will get better after the midterms. But by the looks of his dismal polling numbers, not many people are swallowing his empty promises anymore.

news.title: ‘Refusing to meet Trump was an easy no’: Colin Kaepernick on being ‘blackballed’ for taking the knee, racism, and why he’s still ready to play
news.text:
Colin Kaepernick still gets up at 4.30am every morning to train. “Strength training, speed training, position training – still do all of the same type of workouts I did while I was playing,” he says cheerily. “And then go about the rest of my day.” It is almost 10 years since Kaepernick last played a game of top-flight football. His career was abruptly and cruelly cut short just as it was peaking, after the National Football League (NFL) effectively closed ranks and shut him out for being too political. Now, at 38 years old, he is well aware that his chances of a return are dwindling by the day, but he remains as game-ready as ever. “I stay relentless at it,” he continues in his easy drawl. “I look at it from the perspective of, ‘What are the things that I can control?’ And what I know I can control is being prepared for when opportunity knocks, and to also continue knocking, on my end, looking for ways and opportunities … just staying resilient and focused and disciplined – that is what’s gotten me to this point in my life.”

Kaepernick’s story is defined by the events of late 2016, when he repeatedly refused to stand for the pre-game national anthem – resulting in a chorus of booing on the pitch, insults and outrage off it, and exclusion from the sport he still loves. He was one of the biggest names in the game at the time; quarterback for the San Francisco 49ers, a national celebrity, sponsored by major brands, and looking back, his actions fed into so much that has happened since: the rise of Donald Trump, the Black Lives Matter protests and a global reckoning with racism, then the backlash against what is now being called “Woke 1.0”, and the resurgence of a white nationalism that the US complacently assumed was in the past.

Through all of this, Kaepernick has largely held his silence. He has rarely spoken to the media and restrained from making public statements. Why so, I ask. Surely there must have been times he’s wanted to speak out?

“Oh, absolutely,” he replies. “But I go back to, like, what am I trying to accomplish by doing so?” The temptation to rebut all the lies, the bad takes, the accusations was great, he admits, but, “I realised that, coming out of the protests in 2016, there was a lot of movement and effort made to try to make it as if I was the singular voice in this space doing work, and I was the person solely leading this movement, and that’s just not the reality.”

In person, Kaepernick is friendly and relaxed, speaking on a videocall from his agent’s office in New York (understandably, he doesn’t like to disclose where he lives or spends his time). Even when he’s talking about the worst moments in his life, which is most of the time in our 90-minute conversation, his face defaults to a smile and he’s quick to laugh. He’s looking as dapper as ever: black dress shirt, top button done up; neatly trimmed facial hair; his voluminous afro a work of tonsorial topiary.

The reason Kaepernick is talking now is because he has a new memoir: The Perilous Fight, which details his upbringing, his illustrious sporting career, and the events leading up to and from that pivotal moment in his life. This is not Kaepernick closing off a chapter of his life, he insists, he just felt that now was the time to speak up: “It’s important for where society is, where we’re at as a country, and some of the direction that the world’s heading in, to be able to continue to move things forward.” Also, he says, “we’re coming up on the 10-year anniversary. So a lot things just naturally aligned.”

He doesn’t need to clarify the anniversary he’s referring to. Kaepernick’s decision to protest was the culmination of “a lifetime of experiences of being Black in America,” he says. But in the moment, it was also spontaneous: “It is not something I discussed with anyone else. It was a personal belief and conviction, and originally I did it not knowing or thinking anybody would see or ask about it,” he says. He didn’t even tell his then fiance (now wife), Nessa Diab. The first three times he did it, hardly anyone noticed. At the 49ers’ preseason game in Santa Clara, California, on 14 August 2016, Kaepernick did not take the knee; he simply sat on a cool box during the pre-game Star-Spangled Banner. He was recovering from injury and not dressed for the game, so he was inconspicuous. He did the same thing for the next two games.

By the third time, NFL Network reporter Steve Wyche (who is Black) had clocked it, and spoke to Kaepernick about it. Wyche had also noticed that Kaepernick had been posting all year on his social media about Malcolm X, Martin Luther King Jr, Muhammad Ali, Black Panther co-founder Huey P Newton and Tupac Shakur. That January, for example, he had posted a quote from Dr King: “He who accepts evil without protesting against it is really cooperating with it.”

Kaepernick had certainly been on a journey in terms of his Black history education, partly thanks to Diab – who, a few years earlier, had given him a copy of Malcolm X’s autobiography and told him he’d be “for ever changed”. But his decision to act was also motivated by recent police killings of innocent Black men: Mario Woods, shot and killed by five officers in December 2015 in San Francisco, where Kaepernick was living at the time, using what was later judged “unnecessary force”; Alton Sterling, shot and killed in Louisiana in July 2016; Philando Castile, shot and killed in Minnesota the day after Sterling’s death.

“You then get to a point of, if you understand the problem and you understand the reality and you understand the experience, you either look at yourself in the mirror and say, ‘I’m gonna take action and try to do something about it’, or, ‘I’m not going to, and I’m going to be complicit in this’,” he says. The reality had become clear to him: that “the United States is not a representation of my ideals and my beliefs and has not been representing myself or the Black community. And that has been true since its inception.”

By the time Kaepernick took the knee for the first time, at the suggestion of his team-mate Eric Reid, who knelt alongside him, the issue had become a global news story. He, Reid and others continued to kneel through that season, often to boos and chants of “USA! USA!” Opponents accused Kaepernick of disrespecting the flag, the country, the military, and law enforcement, repeating the familiar mantra that politics should be kept out of sport. People began selling T-shirts outside football stadiums showing him in the scope of a rifle or telling him to, “Shut up and stand up!” Social media posts against Kaepernick turned vicious and racist. He began to receive death threats, including letters sent to his home address. Unfamiliar cars would park outside the entrance to his and Diab’s house, within a gated community. He temporarily moved out, for their safety.

Trump, then a presidential candidate, seized on the controversy: “I think it’s a terrible thing. And maybe he should find a country that works better for him,” he told a radio interviewer. Steve King, at the time a Republican congressman, invoked Diab’s Egyptian heritage to argue that “this is activism that’s sympathetic to Isis”. President Obama’s response was different: “I think he cares about some real, legitimate issues that have to be talked about,” he told reporters.

Kaepernick felt largely supported by his immediate teammates; less so by the NFL as an institution. By the end of the 2016 season, by which time dozens of other players had joined in the knee-taking, it had become clear to him they were “trying to get rid of me”, he believes. In February 2017, the 49ers’ new coach and general manager gave him a choice: he could opt out of his contract now, or they would cut him later – knowing that if he left later, his chances of signing for another team would be greatly reduced. In other words, they were pushing him out, but wanted to make it look like he was leaving of his own volition. “It was a cowardly way for them to handle it,” he says.

Kaepernick was “both surprised and not” by the response. “History tells us that a reaction like this is likely to take place. At the same time, because I have a belief that people are fundamentally good and want to do right, I was amazed at how visceral the response was to saying we shouldn’t be killing Black people. It is almost unfathomable to me that that is something that’s a debate in this country. And on the back of that was a realisation of: good, we need to have this conversation. It made it very clear where a lot of people’s beliefs lay, which then became a much more honest place to be. And there really wasn’t a whole lot of middle ground.”

It must have been an alienating experience, I suggest. Were there times when it all got to him?

“The same way it revealed a lot about society at large, it also revealed a lot about the people around me,” he replies. He talks of how it led to deeper relationships, new friendships, an expanded community. “So while a lot of the immediate reaction is, ‘Oh here was all of the backlash and all of the things that were difficult’, it’s also, ‘Here are all of the great things that came out of this.’ Both of those exist, but we have to put things in perspective. Maybe that’s the eternal optimist in me: I like to look at things through the lens of ‘these are opportunities to get better’.”

You are relentlessly positive, aren’t you, I say to him. He laughs. “I try to be! That’s not to say that that negative thing doesn’t exist, but I don’t want to just live in that negative thing. I think there’s always a solution, and a way forward.”

If there is any middle ground to occupy when it comes to race issues in the US, Kaepernick could make a pretty good claim to it. His racial identity is more complicated than it appears. He was born to a Black father and a white, teenage mother, and was adopted at five weeks old by a white family from Wisconsin (he has never met his biological parents). Rick and Teresa Kaepernick were conservative, church-going, Republican-leaning. Rick was a manager for a cheese company. They already had a son and a daughter, but had lost two sons due to heart defects and were eager to have another one, irrespective of race. So Kaepernick grew up in predominantly white communities, first in Wisconsin, then, from age four, in Turlock, California.

As such, his early experiences of being Black in the US were largely as an isolated individual, often made more acute by his parents’ lack of understanding or even awareness of his racial difference. “They came in with a perspective of, ‘Hey, if we do things the same way we did with my brother and sister, everything will be OK’, and that just wasn’t the case.”

Growing up Black in a white community had its advantages, he says. “You get to see and experience a lot of things that otherwise may not reveal themselves. There was a level of comfort there of like, ‘Oh well, if this Black boy is in this white family, he must have assimilated into some of the white perspectives and cultural elements. That makes it OK for us to talk freely and openly in front of him.’ You get a lot of valuable insights into people’s true perspectives, and it gives you a better understanding of how to be able to navigate that.”

But he was often treated very differently when strangers did not realise he was his parents’ son. In his memoir he recounts how, aged eight, he was tied to a tree by some older white kids in his neighbourhood, who called him the N-word and told him to “go back to Niger”.

Kaepernick’s youthful attempts to connect with Black culture did not always go down well with his parents, either. When he first got his hair braided in cornrows, like his hero, basketball star Allan Iverson, they told him: “You look like a thug.” They were happier when he brought home a white girlfriend than when he brought home a Black one. There were a lot of arguments, he says, over his taste in hairstyles, clothes, music. “But what I will say is, the areas that there was no question around were the idea of being a moral person and doing the right thing and treating people well … The foundational piece is, I know my parents love me as their son.”

Sport was one route to connecting with his racial identity. He was outstanding from a young age – as talented at pitching a baseball as throwing a football, and a pretty good basketball player, too. As he ascended the ranks of school and college football, he came into contact with more Black peers. He also experienced the US’s racially charged law enforcement first-hand. As a teen he was pulled over and given a ticket driving his mother’s convertible with three Black friends – “driving while Black”, he jokes. Another time, at college, the cops pulled guns on his Black roommates, who were helping someone move; they had assumed it was a burglary.

But Kaepernick’s discipline and commitment began to pay off: by the time he turned pro, in 2011, he was already a clear talent. The following season he led the 49ers to the Super Bowl (they lost to the Baltimore Ravens). He was one of the best “dual-threat” quarterbacks in the league – as effective running with the ball as he was passing it. In many respects, before 2016, he was living the footballing dream: he was rich, famous, one of the biggest stars in the game. He had a glamorous girlfriend (Diab was hosting a hip-hop radio show and appearing on MTV), big-name sponsors like Nike, was on the cover of magazines. “Suddenly, I was everywhere all at once,” he recalls.

As much as he still loves the sport, Kaepernick’s protest changed his relationship to it, almost irreparably. And as much as he sought to expose racism in policing, he exposed it within football. More than 70% of NFL players are Black, but historically, team owners and coaches have been overwhelmingly white, and there have been mechanisms in place to keep it that way. In his book, Kaepernick likens the NFL’s scouting combine, where college players are assessed by NFL teams with a series of physical tests and demeaning medical assessments, to a slave market. He recounts how commodified players often are, how their injuries are often glossed over in the interests of short-term results, even how Black players’ baseline intelligence is assumed to be lower than that of white players, which makes it harder for them to claim medical benefits for brain injuries later on. “It is something that historically we will look back on as a society like, how did we ever let that fly? The same way that we ask, how did we ever allow slavery or Jim Crow to happen?”

After he left the 49ers in 2017, no other team picked him up. Other players who protested had similar experiences, including Reid, even as scores more continued to take the knee. Trump, by then president, told a rally that he’d love to see NFL owners respond by saying: “Get that son of a bitch off the field right now. Out! He’s fired.” Many of those owners were his people: white, Republican-leaning billionaires. Some were friends and direct supporters, including New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, the Dallas Cowboys’ Jerry Jones, and Miami Dolphins’ Stephen Ross (who held a fundraiser for Trump in 2019).

Kaepernick believes the NFL made an example of him: “By blackballing me, denying me employment because of fighting to create a better society and fighting to keep people alive, there’s very real implications about who they are as an organisation and what they believe. I think, largely, the community and society knows it and sees it,” he says.

In October 2017, he sued the NFL for “collusion” in shutting him out in retaliation for his activism. The NFL settled out of court in February 2019 for an undisclosed sum. Kaepernick has signed a non-disclosure agreement so cannot go into details, he says, although he would be “very open to the NFL releasing all the documentation and letting society decide”. But he clearly regrets the way things panned out: “I was not protesting the NFL; I was protesting what was happening directly in communities and Black people being killed by police. And the NFL inserted themselves within that conversation and took a side.” (NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has denied Kaepernick was blackballed, saying personnel decisions are made by individual teams.)

As well as being the 10th anniversary of Kaepernick’s protest, it is also, of course, 10 years since the arrival of Trump on the political scene. Their fates seem intertwined: Trump capitalised on Kaepernick’s protest to whip up political support, then his associations with NFL owners helped shut Kaepernick out of the sport. What would Kaepernick say to Trump if they met?

“Well here’s the funny part,” he says breaking into a broad grin. “My lawyers got a phone call with him asking for me to come in to a meeting, I believe it was 2017 or 2018.” There was not a lot of clarity around why Trump wanted to meet him, but it was “a very easy no”, he says. “I am willing to work with anyone who has a genuine interest in creating a better environment and a more equitable society. I do not think that is the case there. I would be curious why there would even be a call and what the topic would be beyond trying to do a photo op.”

Within a few tumultuous years, Kaepernick’s stance began to look less controversial. The Black Lives Matter movement had already begun before he started kneeling, but by 2020 the catalogue of police killings of innocent and unarmed Black men, many of them captured on video, had become intolerable. The murder of George Floyd, in Minneapolis in May 2020, was a tipping point, sparking huge anti-racism protests worldwide. As a consequence, players began taking the knee across US sports – football, basketball, baseball, soccer, hockey – at every level, from high school upwards. In England, football players began to take the knee before kick-off for every game, including the national team. Sportspeople and public figures across the world joined in. Where Kaepernick had once knelt virtually alone, now he had inspired a global gesture. He takes no credit for what happened, simply observing that, when it comes to highlighting police brutality, “there are people that have been doing work on the ground directly in communities for years and decades, and a lot of this bubbled up and came to fruition and got elevated during this moment”.

In terms of the so-called “racial reckoning” that ensued in the immediate aftermath of 2020, he observes that “people and organisations were pledging large sums of money to address everything but police brutality. A lot of it became about businesses using the moment to further their interests.” There was some radical reassessment of racial attitudes on all levels – societal, political, corporate – but there was also a lot of political virtue-signalling, such as house speaker Nancy Pelosi, Kamala Harris and other Democrats taking the knee in the Capitol in June 2020, scarves of kente cloth around their shoulders. The then Labour leader Keir Starmer and deputy leader Angela Rayner also performatively knelt, as did many others. Even some progressive politicians cringe at the recollection now. We are speaking shortly before Alexandrio Ocasio-Cortez gave her assessment that “Woke 1.0 was crazy” – suggesting that progressives went too far, post-BLM. This comes on top of ongoing efforts by Trump to roll back all manner of civil rights and inclusion advances: removing high-ranking Black officials from the military; allowing immigration officials to target Black and brown people; effectively operating a whites-only immigration policy. It is sometimes difficult to see what progress has been made. What does it say, for example, that Trump is still in power, a decade on?

“It says we have a long way to go,” Kaepernick acknowledges. But as ever, he accentuates the positive: “I also think, within that, it has created such a clear and stark reality for so many people that they are rejecting the politics of the administration and looking for something that actually serves everyone.”

This is where Kaepernick’s energy is focused: building the movement. He may have been quiet but he has been busy over the past decade. His Know Your Rights Camp tours the country teaching young people “not just how to survive but also how to thrive”. His charity funds legal assistance and independent autopsies for those who need it (including the family of Nolan Wells, the Black Mississippi teenager who died in mysterious circumstances on a trip with his white friends this July). He runs a publishing company, and has donated over $1m to community projects. He’s thinking in terms of Ella Baker, the relatively unsung activist who laid the foundations for America’s civil rights movement, from the 1930s onwards. “That was centred around: yes, we need strong leaders, but we need strong people, and how do we elevate more people to become leaders so this truly becomes a movement?”

Progressive politics is making a comeback, he says, especially within younger generations. “When we think about gen Z and gen Alpha, they’re very much coming from a perspective of, ‘Do you represent my beliefs? Do you represent who I am? And if you don’t, we’re not going to support you’ … As more and more pressure is able to be exerted from the ground up, I think those high-level conversations and positionings are going to start shifting and swinging as well.” He has a four-year-old daughter now, he adds, describing her as “relentlessly fierce”: “Being a father heightens the sense of urgency.”

Given all this, isn’t Kaepernick more an activist than a sportsman now?

“I look at myself as multi-faceted,” he says. “I still love playing football. I still train for it, make sure that I’m ready and prepared. I also care deeply about people. And if that gets framed as being an activist, by all means, great, let’s do that. But at the core of it, I think people should be able to live, they should be able to thrive, they should able to have dignity, have justice, and that should extend to everyone.”

Kaepernick was always mindful of the roll call of Black sportspeople who took a stand for civil liberties and paid a price for it, he says. “That was something I was aware of prior to ever protesting.” Muhammad Ali refused to be drafted into the Vietnam War and was stripped of his heavyweight boxing title. Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised their fists in Black Power salutes on the podium at the 1968 Olympics, which effectively ended their sprinting careers. Curt Flood challenged the “reserve clause”, which prevented baseball players from choosing their own fates, in 1969, and forfeited his career. More recently basketball player Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf, refused to stand for the national anthem throughout the 1995-96 season, for similar reasons to Kaepernick, and was suspended and fined by the NBA as a consequence.

Kaepernick has had a few tryouts with interested teams, most recently in 2022 with the Las Vegas Raiders – their head coach told him, “You look bigger, faster, stronger than when I last saw you,” Kaepernick says. But the longed-for return has not happened. Is there a part of him that accepts his sporting career may be over? “We don’t have to accept that as the reality,” he replies. “There’s an opportunity to change that … so that when an athlete or when someone speaks up to try to create a better life and better future for a people, for a community, for society, they aren’t met with exile, but they’re actually embraced and people say, ‘You know what, you’re right. Let’s take the actions to actually make this better.’ When we can lay that foundation, that creates significant opportunity for change.”

So he will continue to train, he says. “I will not let go of that as a discipline, as part of who I am.”

If he was back on an NFL team again, would he still take the knee for the national anthem?

“Absolutely,” he says. “The work still needs to be done. More people need to be brought into that work and into that conversation. And more people need to be taking action around it. And I will continue to do the work. I will continue to protest because, quite literally, people’s lives are at stake.”
news.summary:

news.title: The Great Republican Panic Is Upon Us
news.text:
Welcome to this weekend’s edition of the Surge, Slate’s politics newsletter. Oh, you think it’s “bad” or “completely and obviously illegal” that Donald Trump has used taxpayer dollars to air a campaign-season ad celebrating himself while the lyric “love me” plays repeatedly in the background? Sounds like you’ve got Trump Derangement Syndrome, cowpoke.

We are little more than a month from the stupid midterms, and Republicans Are in Disarray. They were specifically promised that the Iran war would not have trade-offs! Susan Collins is not concerned about a major story that dropped this week, but perhaps she should be. Plus, why do some Democrats keep describing one New York Republican House member as unbeatable? He may be with that attitude.

First up, though: If you’ve got some diesel sitting around the house, you could make a pretty penny on Facebook Marketplace.

The week Republicans in red states realized they’re going to have to hustle.

Everyone has understood for some time that this would be a favorable election cycle for Democrats. But this seemed to be the week that this passive knowledge blew into true panic for Republicans—in red states.

The Iran war raised energy prices since its inception. But it’s the recent price spike of diesel fuel, late in campaign season, that’s driven Republicans into a previously unseen fit of panic. A diesel price spike isn’t good for anyone who enjoys such things as, say, eating food or purchasing products. But it’s especially bad for big agricultural states, where margins were already thinned due to tariffs and fertilizer prices. Indeed, one of the truly unusual features of the Trump administration has been how the president has so specifically worked to make people’s lives difficult in places like, say, Iowa and Kansas.

Well, Iowa and Kansas have a bunch of races this year, and the candidates are abruptly sounding different. Rep. Ashley Hinson, running for Senate in Iowa against Democrat Josh Turek, posted this week that “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end,” while Iowa GOP Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks went a step further and actually voted to end the war last week. All are in competitive races, and one poll this week showed Hinson trailing Turek by 8 points. This was a bit of an outlier, but the race shouldn’t be especially competitive to begin with. In Kansas, meanwhile, Sen. Roger Marshall—running against Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton in an ever-closer race—separated himself from the president by chastising Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s behavior in the state. Marshall has continued voting for the Iran war, and Hamilton is hammering him over it.

How deep will this red-state incursion go? Already, national Republicans have all but given up purple-state Senate races like Georgia and North Carolina, as more and more money will have to go to defensive measures in Texas, Ohio, Alaska, Iowa, and Kansas. Nebraska? Maybe South Carolina and Mississippi? As National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott told GOP senators this week, senators in deep-red states need to run as if they’re behind so all resources can go toward the “record number of toss-up races” on the map.

Democrats shouldn’t get overly excited about the prospect of winning, say, eight Senate seats. Republicans still have the money advantage, and their recent deluge of spending should tighten things a bit. Trump will pull some gimmick with diesel prices, like an export ban, that will be terrible policy but might offer relief for a hot second. And many swing voters, while livid at Republicans, still do consider Democrats to be helpless freaks. But this week? Take in the GOP panic. Marinate in it. It is rich. And all because of policy choices—wars, tariffs—that did not need to be made.

Will that story about Susan Collins and the scam defense contractor matter?

Not every Senate race is a vision of unadulterated joy for Democrats. They still have to watch their backs in races where they nominated more-left-wing candidates (Michigan, Minnesota, Maine) or where people might be conflating the Republican candidate with his more popular brother (New Hampshire). In Maine, for example, the Collins machine is still chugging along in a tight race with Troy Jackson, and even led him in a New York Times poll released this week. (Others showed Jackson ahead.)

On Tuesday, though, ProPublica published a much-discussed investigation into the Collins team’s relationship with Martin Kao, the former CEO of a Hawaiian defense contractor. Kao is now in federal prison after his business plan—buying off politicians with campaign donations in exchange for defense contracts that never went anywhere—was exposed. The story reveals that Collins helped secure the company funds while Kao used shell companies to make large donations to Collins’ super PAC. The FBI was supposedly digging deep into the situation until Trump came to office, at which point FBI agents were either fired or reassigned to assisting Homeland Security in the pervasive harassment of immigrants.

The Collins team portrayed it all as a hit piece, saying any notion of a pay-to-play scheme was “categorically false.” Her strongest argument in response to it is that much of it relies on interviews Kao did with the FBI once he was already in jail and looking to save himself, although ProPublica countered that it had independently verified many of his claims. (There are also some not-great emails from members of Collins’ orbit in there.) But even if there’s no hard camera footage of Kao giving Collins burlap sacks full of cash, there is undoubtedly a story that she got duped into delivering federal dollars to a scammer.

One quote that didn’t make it into our feature on Collins earlier this year, but that came back to me this week, was from former Sen. Roy Blunt: “I can’t think of an earmark that Susan has ever asked for that turned out to be a problem for her politically.” That may no longer be the case.

Is Mike Lawler really a brilliant political force of such magnitude that he cannot be defeated?

Last week, moderate, retiring Maine Democrat Jared Golden—who’s really winging it on his way out of office—endorsed New York GOP Rep. Mike Lawler for reelection, citing Lawler’s ability to work with the other side to pass legislation. What caught our eye about this was a reaction from one House Democrat, who told the Washington Sun that Golden’s endorsement didn’t bug them, since “I don’t think Lawler’s beatable.” And this caught our eye because we read the same line from a “senior House Democrat” in an Axios story last month, almost word for word.

Well, these House Democrats—or this one House Democrat who really likes delivering the same line to multiple reporters—are suffering from acute confidence issues, because: what? Sure, Lawler is pretty talented at maintaining his individual brand, either by carving out additional tax relief for his constituents in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year or by calling out bigots within his party. And, sure, Lawler was one of only three House Republicans who won districts in 2024 carried by Kamala Harris. That’s all a testament to his skill, but it’s also a sign that he would be directly underneath a blue wave should it come to crash. As ol’ Bert Camus would say: One must imagine Lawler beatable.

Republicans have put a lot of money behind defending Lawler’s seat, and there’s been some question as to why Democrats haven’t kept up in propping up his opponent, Cait Conley. (Conley is arguably the purest distillation of DCCC recruitment ever: West Point. Military. Harvard. MIT. National Security Council.) But part of the reason they haven’t kept up is because Democrats … don’t have as much money.

For an extra section of lightning-round political thoughts from Jim, sign up to get the Surge in your inbox.
news.summary: These races weren’t supposed to be close. Now they very much are.

news.title: Angie Nixon Proposes Building Data Center on Mar-a-Lago
news.text: Florida Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon believes the country should consider pausing the construction of new artificial intelligence data centers—and jokes that if companies insist on building them, they should start at President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida. Speaking to Newsweek in a wide-ranging interview, Nixon, a state representative who scored an upset victory in Florida's Democratic Senate primary last month, called for greater scrutiny of the rapidly expanding facilities amid concerns about their impact on electricity costs, water supplies and the environment. "I think there needs to be a moratorium until more research is done," Nixon said. "Or if people want to build a data center, they should put it on Mar-a-Lago." The issue is becoming increasingly politically salient as the AI boom drives a surge in proposed data centers across the country. Bipartisan opposition has emerged from communities concerned about their impact on electricity grids, water usage and utility bills. Both Republican- and Democratic-led states have taken or proposed steps—including moratoriums—to address concerns, but Trump has downplayed the widespread unease. The president has repeatedly spoken out against AI regulations, referring to the backlash as a “hoax” and suggesting opposition will result in communities becoming “backwards and poor.” Nixon told Newsweek she was not opposed to AI or technological innovation but wanted tougher guardrails around privacy, employment and the construction of data centers. She also floated a proposal modeled loosely on Alaska's system of distributing revenue associated with its natural resources: requiring or creating a mechanism for communities affected by data centers to receive some form of financial benefit. "Do we do what they do in Alaska, which is like, they give dividends to people who are impacted by the pipeline?" Nixon said. "Do we do the same thing for the now existing AI data centers?" Nixon did not detail how such a program could work, but similar ideas are being considered already. Illinois lawmakers have proposed requiring certain data centers receiving state tax incentives to make payments to host communities, with some of the money benefiting homeowners through payments, credits or rebates, while proposals in New York would provide electricity-bill credits or energy improvements to residents near large data centers. At the federal level, Democratic lawmakers have proposed taxing data centers to offset some of their economic and community impacts. While Nixon's Alaska comparison is not precise—the state's Permanent Fund invests mineral revenues and uses investment earnings to help fund annual dividends—the proposals share the principle of returning some economic benefit to communities affected by major development. Can a Democrat Flip Donald Trump's Home State? Beyond the raging debate over AI, Nixon's campaign is testing whether this year's political environment can make a state that has shifted sharply toward Republicans competitive again. Trump, who has made Mar-a-Lago his primary residence, won Florida by about 13 percentage points in 2024, taking nearly 56 percent of the vote compared with Democrat Kamala Harris' roughly 43 percent. Republicans also now hold a commanding voter-registration advantage. As of August 31, Florida had about 5.65 million active registered Republicans compared with 4.10 million Democrats—a gap of more than 1.5 million voters. The Cook Political Report currently rates the Florida Senate race Solid Republican, underscoring the scale of Nixon's challenge. The Sabato Crystal Ball shifted the race in the Democrat's favor this week from "likely Republican" to "lean Republican," Recent polling has produced a range of results—including two recent survey showing a dead heat. A St. Pete Polls survey of 913 likely voters, conducted September 15-17, found Republican Senator Ashley Moody and Nixon effectively tied, 45.2 percent to 44.8 percent. A Change Research poll earlier in September also put the candidates at 47 percent each, although that survey was conducted for the Democratic-aligned Freedom Project USA. Other surveys have shown Moody with a clearer advantage. Quantus Insights put her ahead 50.1 percent to 42.7 percent, while an InsiderAdvantage survey conducted September 20-21 found Moody at 49.3 percent and Nixon at 41.8 percent. Another poll released this week by Stetson University Center for Public Opinion Research showed the Republican ahead by 11 points, 51 percent to the Democrat's 40 percent. There have also been signs this year that Florida voters are at least willing to cross traditional partisan lines in lower-turnout contests. In March, Democrat Emily Gregory won a special election for Florida House District 87, which includes Mar-a-Lago, defeating Trump-endorsed Republican Jon Maples by roughly 51 percent to 49 percent. Trump had carried the district in 2024. Democrat Brian Nathan separately flipped a Florida state Senate district that Trump had won by about 7 points. Those results came amid a broader national environment that has recently favored Democrats. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in September found Democrats holding an 8-point advantage over Republicans among Americans asked which party they would support in the midterms, while Trump's approval rating stood at 32 percent. Democrats have also consistently overperformed in a slate of off-year and special elections across the country since Trump returned to office for his second term. Republicans nevertheless enter November holding a 53 to 47 Senate majority, including the two independents who caucus with the Democratic side. Democrats, therefore, need a net gain of four seats to reach 51 if the rest of the map remains unchanged. Florida, however, is not currently considered among the central battlegrounds. A Nixon victory would signal a significant victory for Democrats, demonstrating that the Southern state increasingly viewed as a pro-Trump Republican stronghold is still in play. A Democratic Socialist, But Not Really a Socialist Nixon's membership in the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) is another possible headwind the Senate candidate is seen by many to face. Florida is home to large communities of Cubans, Venezuelans and other Latin Americans, many of whom themselves fled, or grew up in families that fled socialism and communism. Moody has capitalized on these factors in her bid to get Florida voters behind her reelection campaign. "The rise of Marxist organizations promoting communism should scare every American," the Republican incumbent wrote on X Friday. She urged Floridians to vote in the November midterm to prevent socialism from taking "root in our country." Nixon joined the DSA in June but has repeatedly said she does not consider herself a socialist and does not agree with the organization's entire platform. She has specifically rejected calls to defund the police or abolish prisons, while supporting ending for-profit prisons. Asked by Newsweek why she joined the organization despite rejecting the socialist label, Nixon pointed to its support for policies including universal healthcare, public education and affordable housing. She noted that she also joined the Working Families Party and became a lifetime NAACP member around the same period. "For me, it was all hands on deck," Nixon said. "We have the ultra wealthy getting richer and richer and richer, and meanwhile, the rest of us are just breaking." Pressed on whether the DSA affiliation could hurt her with Florida's Cuban and Venezuelan communities, Nixon said she would not "insult the intelligence of the voters." "They're smart and they do their research," she said, arguing Republicans were attempting to exploit voters' fears about socialism. Moody has sought to make Nixon's DSA membership a defining contrast in the race. The issue has followed Nixon since her primary victory, and she said again this week that the campaign was "not about three letters," referring to DSA. "There is no place in America that better understands the true cost of socialism and communism than Miami," Moody posted on social media earlier this month. "OUR FREE State of Florida will tell the Socialist Squad’s newest recruit, Angie Nixon, her destructive policies have no place in Florida," the Republican wrote. Angie Nixon's Criticism of the Democratic Establishment Nixon also offered pointed criticism of her own party. Asked whether national and state Democrats were providing enough assistance after her primary victory, Nixon said they "could definitely give me more support." "It's true what my husband has said sometimes," she added. "The Democratic Party and the Republican Party, they're just two different wings on the same bird." Nixon said that some Democratic leaders receive money from the same interests that fund Republicans, adding that her own reliance on small-dollar donations made her a "threat" to that system. She also noted, however, the support she has received from prominent Democratic senators and progressive leaders, naming Senators Lisa Blunt Rochester, Kirsten Gillibrand, Bernie Sanders, Elizabeth Warren and Cory Booker. Her criticism comes amid broader tensions within the Democratic Party ahead of November, particularly between progressive candidates and more establishment-aligned Democrats in several competitive races. While Democrats have overperformed in recent elections, there has been a strong strain of anti-establishment energy, with young and often more progressive candidates winning notable victories against incumbents. This movement has also pointed its frustration at key Democratic leaders, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. Some progressives have already begun calling for Schumer's ouster as leader. For her part, Nixon declined to commit to supporting Schumer but also did not rule it out. "I'm going to run this race, I'm going to win, and then I'm going to assess who I want to vote for leader," she said. "And so it is going to be based on the vision that the folks have." Affordability Is Angie Nixon's Central Message Nixon repeatedly returns her messaging to affordability concerns, saying that economic frustration could allow her to reach Floridians who previously supported Trump. Asked to identify three policies that would most directly lower household expenses, Nixon pointed to universal healthcare, repealing tariffs and universal childcare. "People are going bankrupt because they're trying to stay alive," she said while advocating for universal healthcare. On tariffs, Nixon described them as a tax on working families and argued that repealing them would reduce prices on everyday goods. She also contended that universal childcare would allow parents who left the workforce because of high childcare costs to return. Nixon also called for eliminating federal taxes on Social Security benefits and recounted watching her 70-year-old mother return to work after retiring because her benefits did not stretch far enough. "My mom's 70 years old and she should be enjoying her retirement," Nixon said. "She's worked her entire life." Asked whether Trump had enacted any policy that she believed benefited working-class Americans, Nixon offered one concession: "Eggs are lower than what they were." "That is the only thing that that man has done," she added, before criticizing the rest of his economic record. Trump and Republicans have argued that their tax, trade and economic policies are designed to boost domestic production, increase investment and benefit American workers. Moody's campaign has sought to tie Nixon to the left wing of the Democratic Party, criticizing her agenda and warning that her economic vision would lead the country down a dangerous path. On Gaza and Israel Nixon also reiterated a position that puts her firmly on the progressive side of one of the Democratic Party's most divisive foreign policy debates. She told Newsweek she does not currently support sending U.S. money to Israel. "At this moment, no, I do not support sending any money over to Israel," Nixon said. She called for aggressive diplomacy and said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "needs to go," while arguing that Israelis and Palestinians must ultimately be brought together in pursuit of peace. Pressed on concerns from Jewish and pro-Israel Democrats who view some anti-Israel rhetoric as antisemitic, Nixon drew a distinction between criticism of the Israeli government and hostility toward Jewish people. "I push back on anti-Semitism," she said. "I believe Israelis have a right to exist." "It's not anti-Semitic if I'm upset at their leadership," Nixon added. "I'm also upset at Donald Trump and his leadership in the administration. That does not make me anti-American." Despite her sharp criticism of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), Nixon said she would work with Democratic colleagues who accept support from the pro-Israel group if doing so helped advance policies she believes would benefit Floridians. Taking Aim at Ashley Moody and Donald Trump Throughout the interview, Nixon repeatedly targeted Moody, dubbing her "AI Ashley Moody" and accusing the Republican senator of siding with corporations and wealthy interests. Nixon also argued that Trump had sold working-class voters a "pipe dream" and said some who backed him were now reconsidering their support amid frustration over costs. But despite her repeated criticism of the president, Nixon rejected the idea that her campaign is primarily anti-Trump. "I'm not pushing an anti-Trump message," she said. "I'm pushing a message about how people should decide what their economies and communities look like." Her argument is that voters who may disagree with her ideologically could nevertheless be persuaded by an economic message centered on healthcare, housing, childcare and the cost of living. Whether that can overcome Florida's pronounced Republican shift remains an open question. The state's registration numbers, recent statewide election results and independent race ratings all favor Moody. But Nixon is betting that the same voter dissatisfaction that has helped Democrats in special elections—including in the district surrounding Trump's own Florida home—can make a race few expected to be competitive considerably closer in November. news.title: The High Priests of Performative Goodness
news.text:
I am wary of performative goodness. A few days ago, I wrote in The American Spectator about a speech UN Secretary-General António Guterres had just delivered. Calling him an idiot didn’t quite satisfy me, even though it is a reasonably accurate description of the man. So today, I would like to move beyond the individual (Guterres) and elevate him to a category; that is, to address everyone like him, those who belong to what I often call the postmodern Left: the faction that brought us “wokeism,” a myriad of pronouns, and cardboard straws to countries that had already discovered the immense progress represented by plastic straws. 

The entire ideological structure of the postmodern Left rests on a single moral principle: we are the good guys (kind, benevolent, and big-hearted), while the rest are the bad guys. Their speeches are increasingly unfit for diabetics. They bare their fangs and behave like hyenas only when discussing dissidents (those who hold differing opinions) or whenever they speak of Donald Trump, regardless of what he does or says.

Their goodness reeks just as much as their self-righteousness. One of the things I love most about being Catholic is that, in Christianity, the “good” person is one who denies himself, makes sacrifices, and sometimes even lays down his life for others. Couldn’t the Left do the same? In the postmodern Left, the “good” person sacrifices absolutely nothing (except common sense). They practice charity with your money and mine, imposing peace (a false peace) by abandoning thousands of people who may well need help to the mercy of some authoritarian tyrant, or by encouraging gender transition without taking responsibility for the psychological problems that the victim and their family must face in order to break free from the perpetual unhappiness of living a lie.

They say “no to weapons,” “no to wars,” “no to poverty.” They also say more ambitious things like “no to climate change,” which is like saying “no to the law of gravity.” Their typical solution never solves the problem: their way of fighting poverty is to make the rich poor too, just as their way of fighting academic failure is to make sure every student fails. And the best part, as I’ve noted before: they never take responsibility for the consequences of their stupid ideas. They are like a defective AI developed by AOC: it doesn’t matter what you ask; when something goes wrong, the blame always lies with capitalism or the patriarchy, and “if you want, I can give you a tone that’s a bit more anti-capitalist or a bit more anti-patriarchy.” (RELATED: Why All Leftism Is Now Far Left)

Above all, what really grates on my nerves is that air of the secular saint they adopt, as if they were born in a sacristy (or, in their case, a Masonic lodge), always believing their words are inspired by the Holy Spirit of Marx or a divine breath from Lenin’s mummy. Naturally, they are incapable of admitting a single mistake, except when they happen to be right by accident. In practical terms, they are an adolescent with pretensions of being an intellectual.

It makes no difference whether you read them in The New York Times with the fancy title of full professor hanging on their office wall, or hear them struggling to articulate an opinion on CNN, or watch them drone on with a tedious speech at the U.N. General Assembly, or run into them at a bar holding forth with their own personal “Epistle to the Corinthians.” They combine exaggerated virtue with ridiculous arrogance. And their arrogance is inversely proportional to their reasoning. That is to say, the more idiotic the argument (perhaps because they know it is weak), the more zealously, violently, and irrationally they defend it. (RELATED: The Moral Blackmailing of the American People) 

And the issue of irrationality is another matter of interest. For all its many flaws, the classical Left used to position itself as the champion of reason and science, often pitting them against faith, which they scorned, as they always feel compelled to scorn the beliefs of others. The postmodern Left, however (figures like Kamala Harris or Joe Biden), views reason as a hindrance and regards science as downright fascist, simply because mathematical results fail to align with the tenets of equity, diversity, and equality. (RELATED: No Kings, Except for Progressive Ones)

After all, the only argumentative driving force they constantly invoke is emotion, the heart. Yet, whether the issue is abortion or tax hikes on the middle class, they never truly show heart when it is actually needed. Their sensitivity is mere sentimentality, and it is selective. They are moved only by the idealized paradigm that exists in their own heads, never by the actual individual; perhaps this is simply because they do not believe in the individual, and with each passing day, they appear increasingly detached from reality.

They sleep soundly because they spend vast sums telling the world just how immensely virtuous they are. That is precisely the specialty of people like António Guterres. Unfortunately, I can never be like them; I shall remain an insomniac for the rest of my life, for personally, I prefer a good war to a bad peace. And I feel not the slightest need to explain to the world whether I am a good man or the most despicable creature on earth.
